Driven by advances in flexible electronics, microfabrication, and artificial intelligence, bioacoustics is revolutionizing sensing and signal processing across health, ecology, and intelligent systems. This review systematically examines key progress in high-performance acoustic sensors (e.g., piezoelectric, triboelectric, MEMS) and acquisition schemes for multiscale biological sounds, ranging from heart tones to plant stress emissions. Furthermore, we delve into advanced methodologies for acoustic signal preprocessing, feature extraction, and classification, with a particular emphasis on the powerful analytical capabilities of multimodal data fusion and deep learning algorithms in complex real-world scenarios. Crucially, although the sensing requirements and biological targets vary drastically across medical, ecological, and agricultural domains, this review establishes a unifying framework centered on the shared physical and algorithmic challenges of bioacoustic information flow. By juxtaposing these diverse fields, the potential strategies for the interdisciplinary integration of sensing methodologies are highlighted. We also critically assess the essential roles of acoustic physical modeling, standardized testing frameworks, and gold-standard databases in evaluating system performance. Finally, the review highlights cutting-edge applications of bioacoustics in human health monitoring, medical diagnostics, human-computer interaction, and precision agriculture. By synthesizing current technological convergences and outlining future trajectories, we provide a comprehensive perspective on the promising directions and pivotal challenges facing bioacoustic research.

Integrated bioacoustics: Sensing, Mechanisms, and Applications
1. Sensing technologies 2. Unifying framework & AI 3. Cross-domain applications

Bioacoustics, as an interdisciplinary field, focuses on the mechanisms underlying the production, propagation, and reception of sounds by living organisms, as well as the functions and significance of these sounds in ecosystems. It integrates theoretical and methodological approaches from acoustics, biology, ecology, and signal processing, deciphering sound signals to reveal patterns of biological behaviors, population dynamics, and environmental changes[1-3]. Its research subjects encompass taxa such as insects,

birds, mammals, and marine organisms, while also extending to acoustic signals from plants and humans[4-6], providing a pivotal tool for investigating biological communication, habitat selection, reproductive behaviors, and organism–environment interactions. In recent years, advances in sensing technologies and computing capabilities have driven innovations in research methodologies[7-9], evolving from traditional spectrogram analysis to the application of machine learning algorithms. This progression has enabled bioacoustics to emerge as a crucial pillar for ecological monitoring, biodiversity conservation, and medical diagnosis.

Physiological acoustics (or biomedical acoustics), a core interdisciplinary subfield bridging bioacoustics and medical health, aims to elucidate the principles governing the generation, propagation, and body surface detection of sound within the human body. Internal human physiological sounds originate from the physiological activities of multiple organs: respiratory sounds arise from pulmonary ventilation, heart sounds are generated by the opening/closing of cardiac valves and blood flow pulsation, speech is formed via vocal cord vibration and vocal tract modulation, and gastrointestinal sounds are induced by gastrointestinal peristalsis[10-12]. When propagating toward the body surface, these signals must penetrate complex biological tissues, including muscle, bone, body fluids, and adipose tissue, encompassing reflection and refraction driven by differences in acoustic impedance, tissue elastic responses dictated by acoustic modulus, and frequencydependent propagation characteristics. Specifically, high-frequency sound waves undergo rapid attenuation and shallow penetration due to tissue absorption and scattering, whereas low-frequency sound waves exhibit slow attenuation and tend to resonate within body cavities[13-15]. A defining feature of human physiological signals is their intrinsic association with physiological and pathological states: abnormal organ function alters the generation and propagation pathways of these signals. Precise deciphering of such changes not only provides a noninvasive window for investigating human physiological mechanisms but also lays a theoretical foundation for the early diagnosis, health monitoring, and rehabilitation assessment of disorders (e.g., cardiovascular and cerebrovascular diseases, digestive system diseases). In this regard, physiological acoustics serves as a critical link in translating bioacoustic research into precision medicine.

Bioacoustic monitoring exhibits considerable potential and value in scientific research and practical applications. It provides a noninvasive, efficient method for assessing biodiversity and monitoring ecosystem health. By recording and analyzing environmental sound signals over time, researchers can track species distribution, population dynamics, and habitat quality, offering a robust basis for ecological conservation and environmental management[16-19]. Moreover, bioacoustic technology is instrumental in wildlife conservation, enabling precise monitoring of endangered species’ activity ranges and behavioral patterns through speciesspecific vocalizations, thus supporting evidence-based conservation policies[20-22]. Beyond ecology, bioacoustics shows broad applicability in agriculture, fisheries, and medicine. For example, in agriculture, it facilitates targeted pest control by detecting pest sound signals; in medicine, it aids in studying vocal mechanisms across species, enhancing the diagnosis and treatment of speech disorders[23-25]. These diverse applications not only advance fundamental science but also deliver innovative solutions to real-world challenges.

In recent years, bioacoustics has advanced significantly, propelled by rapid developments in detector technology, signal processing algorithms, and computational power[26,27]. The proliferation of high-sensitivity microphone arrays and autonomous acoustic devices has enabled large-scale, long-term environmental acoustic monitoring[28,29]. Meanwhile, the adoption of AI algorithms has greatly enhanced the precision of sound signal classification and recognition[30,31]. Nevertheless, critical challenges remain. Background noise in complex environments often interferes with target signal isolation, posing a persistent difficulty[32]. Overlapping acoustic traits across species further complicate accurate identification, requiring additional investigation. Moreover, the absence of standardized data-sharing frameworks restricts cross-regional and interdisciplinary collaboration. Finally, the limited alignment between physical models of bioacoustic signals and real biological processes hampers the accuracy of noninvasive monitoring predictions. These unresolved issues not only drive technological innovation but also open broad avenues for future research.

To effectively address the aforementioned challenges and achieve technological breakthroughs, it is particularly urgent to break down the long-standing disciplinary barriers. In most cases, bioacoustic research in the fields of medical health, wildlife ecology, and agriculture tends to operate in isolation due to significant differences in their signal characteristics and evaluation criteria. However, the in-depth integration of flexible electronics and artificial intelligence technologies in recent years has revealed a common underlying technological core across these fields. For instance, whether detecting weak fetal heartbeats or monitoring xylem cavitation in plants under drought stress, “acoustic impedance matching” at the tissue-sensor interface remains a universal physical challenge.

Based on this, this review breaks traditional boundaries and integrates these seemingly disparate fields into a unified framework, systematically summarizing the latest advances in bioacoustic sensing and signal processing technologies. Following the main thread of acoustic information flow, this paper elaborates on the mechanisms of bioacoustic signal generation and propagation, as well as the hardware system covering sensing materials and structural design; it then focuses on the innovative progress in signal preprocessing, feature extraction, and physical acoustic modeling, and highlights the potential of interdisciplinary crossinnovation (e.g., how robust denoising technologies developed for complex marine environments can inspire the design of wearable human diagnostic devices, or how high-sensitivity MEMS architectures in human‒ machine interaction can be transformed into tools for plant health monitoring); furthermore, it discusses the typical applications and existing bottlenecks in fields such as medicine, ecology, and agriculture; finally, it looks forward to frontier directions including the miniaturization of sensing platforms, multisource data fusion, and intelligent algorithms. By synthesizing the above content, this review aims to provide a comprehensive reference for researchers in related fields and effectively build a bridge between basic bioacoustic research and cross-domain practical applications.
2. Characterization and classification of bioacoustic signals
2.1 Classification by biological source and ecological function

The nature and origin of sound exhibit remarkable diversity across biological taxa but fundamentally rely on the physiological basis of mechanical vibration. Bioacoustic signals, characterized by their diverse physical properties and profound biological relevance, have emerged as a focal point of interdisciplinary research. Their systematic classification and characterization not only underpin our understanding of bioacoustic phenomena but also provide a theoretical foundation for the development of advanced sensing and signal processing technologies.

Acoustic signals can propagate through diverse media, including gas, liquid, and solid (Figure 1(a)), and physical parameters such as sound velocity, wavelength, reflection/refraction behaviors, and energy dissipation vary with differences in the mechanical properties (e.g., density, elastic modulus) of the medium during propagation. Based on frequency ranges, acoustic signals are categorized into three major classes: infrasound (<20 Hz), audible sound (20 Hz–20 kHz), and ultrasound (>20 kHz). Infrasound, benefiting from its long-wavelength attribute, is often employed by large-bodied animals (e.g., elephants, whales) for longdistance information transfer; audible sound represents the primary frequency band for intraspecific communication in humans and most terrestrial animals (e.g., birds); and ultrasound plays a pivotal role in processes such as echolocation in bats and navigation in dolphins. As illustrated in Figure 1(b), bioacoustic signals are most effectively categorized by their biological source and ecological function, as these parameters define the underlying sensing requirements. These signals are generally divided into three major classes: human-derived (e.g., physiological sounds), animal-derived (e.g., vocalizations and echolocation), and plantderived signals (e.g., stress emissions). This source-centric classification emphasizes the biological relevance of the acoustic data, ranging from clinical diagnostic biomarkers in humans to behavioral and survival
2.2 Acoustic information flow across biological species

As previously discussed, from the perspective of biological sound sources and ecological functions, bioacoustic signals can be categorized into human-derived, animal-derived, and plant-derived signals (Figure 1(b)). The generation of human physiological signals is closely linked to the anatomical structure and physiological functions of sound-producing organs. For instance, speech arises from airflow-driven vibration of the vocal cords, modulated by resonance in the oral and nasal cavities; in contrast, heart sounds and bowel sounds reflect the physiological activities of the cardiovascular and digestive systems, respectively.

Acoustic signals within the human body and most animals primarily originate from the coupling of viscoelastic tissue motion and multiphase fluid dynamics. These signals propagate through multiple layers of internal media, including deep tissues, muscles, and adipose tissue, before reaching the body surface, where they are ultimately captured by detectors or sensors[10,33]. During propagation, human acoustic signals are shaped by tissue density, acoustic impedance, viscoelasticity, and interstitial fluids, leading to reflection, refraction, attenuation, and frequency-dependent transmission[13,34,35]. Respiratory sounds provide a representative example: they travel through the tracheobronchial tree and surrounding tissues before reaching the chest wall. Because the lung parenchyma strongly attenuates high-frequency components, body-surface respiratory sounds are mainly concentrated in the low-frequency range, making the thoracic cavity behave as a low-pass acoustic filter[36-38]. Heart sounds, generated by valve motion and blood-flow-induced vibration, similarly propagate through multilayer viscoelastic thoracic tissues before being detected at the body surface[11]. Therefore, accurate detection of internal human sounds requires sensor designs and signalprocessing strategies that account for organ-specific sound generation, tissue-mediated propagation, and frequency-selective attenuation.

Beyond the human body, animal acoustic signals also exhibit high diversity and complexity. Their production and propagation mechanisms share certain similarities with those in humans while simultaneously displaying species-specific features. Animal acoustic signals encompass a wide range of modalities, from bird songs to echolocation in marine mammals, reflecting propagation and coupling mechanisms that integrate multiple physical processes[39]. Overall, in both humans and animals, acoustic signals not only serve as tools for information exchange but are also intrinsically linked to survival strategies and social behaviors.

In contrast, the mechanisms underlying acoustic generation and propagation in plants exhibit striking differences from those in humans and animals. Plants lack specialized sound-producing organs; their “acoustic signals” are inherently passive vibrations induced by physiological activities, primarily originating from cavitation events during water transport in xylem vessels (i.e., impacts on vessel walls from bubble collapse or migration), cell division, turgor pressure fluctuations, and tissue vibrations under stress such as herbivory or mechanical stimulation (as shown in the right of Figure 1(b))[40]. Within plants, acoustic vibrations propagate mainly through the vascular system (xylem and phloem) and contiguous cell walls, forming the core pathway for internal vibration signal transmission. Compared to propagation through air or soil, vibrations travel faster within plant tissues (e.g., reaching 3 000–5 000 m·s−1 in xylem) with slower energy attenuation, enabling long-distance signal transmission. Moreover, propagation efficiency is regulated by the plant’s own structure: lignified tissues (e.g., stems, roots) facilitate vibration conduction more effectively than succulent tissues (e.g., leaves, petals), while embolism or disruption of the vascular system due to adverse conditions such as drought significantly impedes vibration transmission. Through the propagation of internal acoustic signals, plants can rapidly transmit local stress signals (e.g., herbivory-induced vibrations perceived by leaves) to roots or other organs, thereby triggering systemic defense responses (such as the synthesis of anti-herbivore proteins and stomatal closure) to adapt to stressful environments.

3. Bioacoustic sensors: from applications to sensor selection

Over the past few decades, the field of bioacoustic sensing has undergone a significant paradigm shift from pursuing universal performance benchmarks to adopting application-specific design principles. This

evolution recognizes that optimal sensor performance must be defined relative to operational contexts rather than abstract metrics. A representative example is cardiac sound monitoring for early diagnosis of heart failure and valvular disorders, where bioacoustic sensors must capture subtle, low-amplitude components such as the third (S3) and fourth (S4) heart sounds in addition to the primary S1 and S2 beats. These low-frequency signals (20–150 Hz) often exhibit tiny amplitudes and are easily masked by respiratory or motion noise, requiring sensors with high sensitivity, flat low-frequency response, superior SNR and good signal postprocessing capability. Moreover, detecting abnormal murmurs or gallops demands a wide dynamic range (30–1 000 Hz) to simultaneously resolve faint pathological events and stronger normal heart tones[41]. Hence, optimal sensor design must balance broad bandwidth with noise suppression while avoiding resonance within the diagnostic band. Such distinct requirements necessitate a more nuanced approach to sensor development.

This section provides a concise overview of the core selection criteria in some specific application scenarios (healthcare, human‒machine interaction (HMI) and agriculture), including benchmarks such as sensitivity, response times, frequency and dynamic range, signal-to-noise ratio (SNR), and resolution. In parallel, system-level metrics such as environmental robustness, directionality, acoustic impedance matching, signal processing integration, biocompatibility, and long-term stability are considered in diverse deployment environments (Figure 2). Establishing these evaluation criteria facilitates more rational selection of sensor mechanisms, materials, and structural designs, thereby promoting systematic and application-specific development of future bioacoustic sensors.

Sensitivity, expressed in mV·Pa⁻¹ or dBV·Pa⁻¹, quantifies the electrical response per unit of sound pressure. In bioacoustic sensing, it should be evaluated in conjunction with dynamic range and frequency bandwidth, as accurate physiological sound detection depends on a balanced trade-off among these parameters. Physiological monitoring presents a clear illustration of these considerations, where the low-frequency components of heart sounds require high sensitivity to detect subtle signals, while the broader frequency distribution is more essential for respiratory noises[42]. These varying characteristics necessitate sensor designs that not only maximize sensitivity but also ensure alignment with the target signals. As such, achieving both high sensitivity and appropriate frequency response constitutes a dual design imperative in the development of acoustic sensors for complex bioacoustic environments. Notably, to achieve a flat frequency response, the resonance frequency of the designed acoustic sensor should be positioned outside the target frequency range. Nevertheless, in specific applications involving a narrowband signal, a tailored resonance band may be
introduced to detect weak acoustic signals[43].

Response time and resolution determine the ability of a sensor to capture transient and subtle acoustic events. A short response time minimizes waveform distortion during rapidly varying signals[44]. High resolution enables the discrimination of small acoustic or mechanical changes associated with physiological or pathological states. However, improved resolution often increases susceptibility to noise, requiring coordinated optimization of sensing materials, device structure, and signal processing[45]. The SNR reflects the distinguishability of target acoustic signals from environmental and circuit noise. A high SNR is essential for detecting weak physiological sounds and ensuring reliable feature extraction. It can be improved through sensor-level response enhancement, acoustic shielding, low-noise front-end circuits, appropriate amplification, and filtering strategies such as power-line interference suppression.

Beyond the core sensing metrics discussed above, several system-level parameters should be considered. Environmental robustness and directionality are critical for bioacoustic sensors used in complex deployment scenarios. Field monitoring requires resistance to dust, wind, water, corrosion, and temperature fluctuations, whereas medical ultrasound, auscultation localization, and voice recognition often benefit from directional sensitivity or array-based spatial discrimination.

Acoustic impedance matching governs the efficiency of acoustic energy transfer across interfaces. In bioacoustic applications, particularly in medical ultrasound and wearable acoustic sensors, the inherent impedance mismatch between conventional sensor materials and biological tissues necessitates strategies such as integrating specialized acoustic windows or employing multilayered gradient-impedance structures. Alternatively, the acoustic impedance of the sensor materials can be tailored by incorporating fiber-reinforced composites or microsphere-embedded architectures that increase porosity to reduce bulk density. Such material modifications effectively reduce intrinsic acoustic impedance, thereby enhancing acoustic coupling efficiency and minimizing reflective losses[46].

Biocompatibility, wearability, mechanical compliance, and long-term stability are essential for wearable and implantable bioacoustic systems. For skin-mounted sensors, especially those used for long-term physiological monitoring, wearability involves stable skin conformity, stretch adaptability, breathability, and comfort during prolonged attachment. Stretch adaptability allows the device to accommodate dynamic skin deformation during breathing, speaking, or daily movement, while breathable substrates or porous encapsulation layers help reduce sweat accumulation and maintain stable acoustic coupling. Hypoallergenic materials are also required to minimize skin irritation, and antibacterial surface coatings may be needed for specific scenarios, such as infant bowel sound monitoring[47]. For implantable or minimally invasive ultrasonic transducers, inert encapsulation and immunological inertness are essential to avoid foreign body responses. For continuous monitoring, electrical and mechanical stability must be maintained through fatigue-resistant structures, material optimization, and protective encapsulation.

Integrated signal-processing capability is increasingly important for intelligent bioacoustic systems. Hardware modules should provide mechanism-specific signal conditioning, low-noise amplification, multichannel synchronization, and wireless transmission. When additional sensors such as IMUs are used for motion-artifact suppression, synchronized multimodal acquisition becomes necessary[48]. On the software side, time-domain, frequency-domain, and ML-assisted analysis can support robust feature extraction and classification, while edge processing with compact MCUs can reduce data transmission and power consumption.

Once the performance requirements under specific application scenarios are identified, the appropriate acoustic sensing mechanisms and active materials can be selected in a more targeted manner, and sensor structures can then be designed accordingly based on the intended parameter ranges (Figure 2). For instance, in applications requiring flexibility and a high-frequency response, piezoelectric polymers such as polyvinylidene difluoride (PVDF) are often prioritized due to their mechanical compliance and fast response. In contrast, bioinspired designs incorporating microstructure piezoresistive sensors can offer frequency

selectivity through structural tuning for artificial cochlear applications[49]. In scenarios demanding spatial resolution, miniaturized sensor arrays are typically realized using microelectromechanical (MEMS) architecture.

Recent advances in bioacoustics have been largely driven by innovations in acoustic transducers capable of capturing weak, low-frequency physiological sounds under dynamic and complex human conditions. Unlike conventional microphones optimized for air-conducted speech, sensors for biomedical monitoring must address distinct challenges, such as low sound pressure (<10 Pa), tissue damping, motion artifacts, and acoustic-impedance mismatch between the sensor and skin. To meet these requirements, research has increasingly focused on flexible and microelectromechanical (MEMS) acoustic sensors that combine high sensitivity, biocompatibility, and long-term stability.

Among diverse transduction strategies, piezoelectric and triboelectric mechanisms are particularly attractive for their potential self-powered operation and high SNR, whereas piezoresistive and capacitive sensors offer simple readout, high sensitivity to small mechanical deformations, and compatibility with flexible wearable architectures[50,51]. Together, these mechanisms dominate current developments in wearable bioacoustic sensing by offering complementary advantages in sensitivity, power consumption, mechanical compliance, and system integration. Meanwhile, electromagnetic and optical sensors, although capable of exceptional sensitivity, remain hindered by bulkiness, alignment complexity, and poor skin conformity. Ultrasonic sensing, extending into the kilohertz–megahertz regime, further enables high-resolution imaging and internal organ motion tracking, bridging the gap between surface acoustics and deep-tissue diagnostics.

In recent years, several high-quality reviews[9,26,27,52,53] have comprehensively summarized the fundamental principles, material systems, structural designs, and fabrication techniques of acoustic sensors, including their emerging applications in bioacoustics and human health monitoring. Therefore, this section does not revisit the transduction mechanisms in detail. Instead, we focus on the recent progress, representative examples, and comparative performance of various acoustic sensor types, emphasizing their practical advantages, limitations, and application prospects in physiological sound detection. By integrating materials innovation, structural engineering, and MEMS-level miniaturization, we aim to elucidate how different sensing strategies evolve toward high-fidelity, flexible, and intelligent platforms capable of long-term wearable bioacoustic monitoring.

3.2.1 Piezoelectric and triboelectric acoustic sensors Piezoelectric transducers have become indispensable in bioacoustic sensing owing to their self-powered operation, rapid response, and efficient electromechanical coupling[54,55]. Their performance is governed by fundamental piezoelectric equations:

Early rigid ceramics such as lead zirconate titanate (PZT) and lead magnesium niobate-lead titanate (PMN-PT) offered high electromechanical coupling but suffered from rigidity and limited skin conformity. Polymeric systems such as PVDF and PVDF-TrFE improved mechanical compliance and are therefore widely used in flexible and wearable acoustic sensors[57,58]. More recently, molecular ferroelectrics have emerged as a promising class of piezoelectric materials for acoustic sensing because they combine high piezoelectric output, structural tunability, low density, and potentially lower acoustic impedance than conventional ceramics. Representative hybrid organic–inorganic molecular ferroelectrics, such as trimethylchloromethyl ammonium trichlorocadmium (TMCM-CdCl₃) and related TMCM-based halide systems, have shown large piezoelectric

coefficients and can be incorporated into polymer matrices to improve flexibility and stretchability. However, their intrinsic brittleness, environmental stability, and large area processability still require further optimization before broad wearable deployment[59].

Device design strongly influences the piezoelectric response; traditional piezoelectric acoustic sensors commonly adopt a sandwich structure, with electrodes placed on both sides of the active layer. Recently, various structural strategies have been employed to amplify mechanical deformation and thus enhance signal output. In bioacoustic applications, thin membranes operate in mixed d₃₁/d₃₃ working modes where in-plane shear stress dominates under acoustic excitation. A typical example is that thermally drawn PVDF fibers doped with barium titanate (BTO) ceramics show a high d₃₁ value (≈ 46 pC·N⁻¹) with anisotropic structures (Figure 3(a)). When woven into acoustic textiles, it can detect nanoscale chest vibrations and sound pressure as low as 10⁻⁷ atm[60]. The bioinspired device also significantly boosted the performance. A printed microcone array based on a lead-free perovskite material mimicking cochlear hair cell geometry achieved 150 mV·Pa⁻¹ sensitivity over 100–3 000 Hz and exhibited directional responsiveness[61]. Beyond thin films, piezoelectric nanofibers with low acoustic impedance further improved conformity and breathability for long-term physiological sound monitoring[62]. Porous piezoelectrets with engineered voids and tunable dipole alignment are gaining attention for their mechanical flexibility and adjustable piezoelectric performance. A porous fluorinated ethylene propylene (FEP) patch incorporating an electromagnetic-shielding layer reduced harmonic interference by > 20 dB and demonstrated reliable detection of heartbeats, respiration, coughing, and swallowing[56]. These examples underscore how material selection and structure design at the micro level reconcile flexibility with high piezoelectric output.

Triboelectric acoustic sensors (TAS) complement piezoelectric systems by generating electrical signals through contact electrification and electrostatic induction. This mechanism involves (1) contact-induced charge transfer between dissimilar materials (characterized by electron affinity differences), (2) separationinduced potential generation and (3) alternating current production through cyclic operation. Their ability to operate without external power and their high voltage output make them promising for voice recognition[63,64], human‒machine interaction (HMI)[65, 66], and health monitoring[67,68].

Early in 2018, a porous FEP/Au-Kapton multilayer TAS was designed to achieve a broadband response from 0.1 to 5 kHz for speech perception[69]. By engineering internal boundaries and spacers, devices later shaped multiresonant behavior to enhance frequency selectivity, extending detection to the full human auditory range for sound localization and tracking[70]. These demonstrations reveal how structure can be intentionally designed to emphasize clinically relevant bands (e.g., 100–1 500 Hz for lung and bowel sounds).

Beyond conventional thin‐film architectures, microstructure engineering has become a key strategy for enhancing triboelectric acoustic sensors. Surface morphology modulation, such as cochlea‐inspired conical micropillar arrays made of PVDF-HFP, effectively enlarges the contact area and amplifies acoustic‐to‐electric conversion, enabling the detection of subtle vibrations within a 50–80 dB range[71]. At the nanoscale, hierarchical and gradient porous composites based on BTNP@SiO₂/PVDF-TrFE systems (Figure 3(b)) provide broadband (145–9 000 Hz) and frequency‐selective responses for noise‐robust voice recognition[72]. Together, these hierarchical designs demonstrate how structural control from micro- to nanoscale enables efficient and selective acquisition of complex acoustic information, paving the way for bioinspired and intelligent sound-sensing platforms.

Overall, both piezoelectric and triboelectric acoustic sensors exhibit excellent adaptability in the bioacoustic frequency range and compatibility with flexible substrates. Piezoelectric devices feature superior linearity and long-term stability, whereas triboelectric devices deliver higher voltage and broader frequency response. The critical challenges ahead lie in suppressing dielectric and charge-leakage noise, improving encapsulation against humidity, and balancing softness with acoustic fidelity for continuous bioacoustic monitoring.

The equation’s first term captures geometric deformation effects, while the second term reflects intrinsic resistivity changes from electronic structure modifications. Their simple readout circuitry and high signal amplitude make them attractive for wearable bioacoustic monitoring, particularly for throat, laryngeal, and speech-related vibrations[78, 79]. Early designs employing doped silicon diaphragms or metallic strain gauges provided linear responses but limited stretchability and low gauge factors, which hindered the detection of faint, lowfrequency biological sounds. Crack engineering in metallic films enhances piezoresistive sensitivity by forming reversible microcrack networks that dynamically modulate conductive pathways under acoustic stress, enabling amplified response to weak vibrations with straightforward fabrication and excellent reproducibility.

The emergence of nanocomposite elastomers incorporating graphene, MXene, or carbon nanotubes (CNTs) has markedly improved flexibility and sensitivity. These conductive networks respond to microstrains induced by acoustic pressure through tunneling and percolation effects, achieving detection thresholds[80, 81]. One representative example is employing polydimethylsiloxane (PDMS) as a flexible elastomeric substrate, embedding regularly arranged micropyramidal structures formed by doping 2D MXene nanosheets into the matrix (Figure 3(c))[73]. Through synergistic geometric and electronic modulation, the MXene–elastomer tympanic membrane realizes hierarchical signal amplification, achieving a 0.1–3 kHz bandwidth and ~50 dB SNR within the key 200–900 Hz range while maintaining a linear acoustic response.

Capacitive acoustic sensors function by transducing mechanically induced vibrations from incident sound waves into periodic fluctuations in capacitance, thereby enabling acoustic perception and signal conversion (𝐶= 𝜖𝐴/𝑑)[82]. Their inherent linearity and scalability through MEMS processing have made them dominant in commercial microphones and increasingly relevant for biomedical applications[83, 84]. These structures suffer from brittleness and fabrication complexity, rendering them less suitable for emerging applications in flexible wearable electronics. To address these limitations, several strategies, such as deformable diaphragms[85, 86], compliant electrodes[80, 87, 88], and soft dielectric layers[89-91] have been developed. Polymeric diaphragms such as polydimethylsiloxane (PDMS), polyimide (PI), or thermoplastic polyurethane (TPU) have replaced rigid silicon to achieve lower acoustic impedance and better skin conformity. The incorporation of electret materials provides built-in polarization, eliminating the need for external bias and reducing power consumption. A representative electret-based membrane achieved sensitivities up to 2.2 V·Pa⁻¹ with a flat 80– 3 000 Hz response, enabling accurate speech and breath detection (Figure 3(d))[74]. Recent designs exploit microstructured diaphragms and compliant electrodes to enhance performance. Corrugated or spring-arm supports relieve residual stress and increase membrane compliance, while graphene or Ag-nanowire electrodes ensure conductivity without sacrificing flexibility[90]. Ionic-gel dielectrics further expand versatility by forming electric double layers that strongly couple with acoustic pressure. Such ionic-
capacitive hybrids exhibit high sensitivity and acoustic-impedance matching with wet or soft tissues, demonstrating potential for underwater and mucosal sound sensing[92].

Comparatively, capacitive sensors deliver a broader frequency range and superior linearity, whereas piezoresistive sensors excel in low-frequency, high-deformation scenarios such as voice, cough, or heartsound monitoring. Both types benefit from MEMS-compatible fabrication, allowing miniaturization and array integration. However, challenges persist. Piezoresistive devices suffer from hysteresis, power drift, and temperature sensitivity; capacitive types require stable biasing and often exhibit reduced output under lowfrequency, small-amplitude vibrations. From a biomedical perspective, the fundamental trade-off lies between mechanical compliance and electrical precision: increasing softness improves comfort but weakens electromechanical coupling.

3.2.3 Optical and electromagnetic acoustic sensors Optical and electromagnetic acoustic sensors represent two high-precision yet nonideal approaches for wearable bioacoustic monitoring. Although both have achieved remarkable sensitivity and frequency response in laboratory or industrial environments, their fundamental physical configurations impose severe limitations on flexibility, miniaturization, and skin conformity, which are critical requirements for human physiological sound detection. Nevertheless, their exceptional stability and noncontact operation render them suitable for nonhuman bioacoustic applications, including the detection of plant acoustic emissions and other lowfrequency biological vibrations.

Optical acoustic sensors transduce sound waves into optical signals by modulating light intensity or wavelength through reflective or interferometric mechanisms. Typical configurations, including intensitymodulated films, fiber Bragg gratings (FBGs), and Fabry Perot interferometers, offer ultrahigh sensitivity and broad bandwidth. Dass fabricated a diaphragm-free microcantilever fiber acoustic sensor (MCM), which realizes low-frequency sound wave detection based on the principle of tapered microtip single-mode fiber light field coupling (Figure 3(e))[75]. This microphone uses a tapered fiber microtip cantilever. Acoustic waves deflect the cantilever, altering the light coupling efficiency with a fixed fiber. It achieves high sensitivity (10.63 mV·Pa−1) in the 0–400 Hz range, which is ideal for low-frequency bioacoustics such as visceral sounds. However, its macroscopic cantilever length limits miniaturization and practical integration for wearable applications. Mechanical fragility and temperature sensitivity are also concerns.

Electromagnetic acoustic sensors generate voltage through electromagnetic induction between a vibrating coil and a magnetic field. Traditional microphones using permanent magnets and wound coils are mechanically robust and capable of broadband operation up to tens of kilohertz, but the necessity of magnetic components inherently results in bulky, rigid structures. When applied to biological monitoring with subtle signals and the dominant frequency lying under 1 kHz, the induced voltage is often in the microvolt range, far below the threshold required for high signal-to-noise detection[26, 93]. Recent works employing microscale coils and flexible NdFeB magnetic films have slightly improved miniaturization and conformability (Figure 3(f)), yet the output remains limited with measurements during chest heartbeat tests yielding approximately 12 microvolts[76]. Furthermore, magnetic hysteresis, temperature drift, and potential interference from external electromagnetic fields complicate stable long-term measurements.

Overall, optical and electromagnetic sensors exemplify the trade-off between measurement precision and mechanical adaptability. Their outstanding sensitivity and bandwidth make them valuable reference technologies for benchmarking signal accuracy or exploring specialized noncontact diagnostics, but their incompatibility with soft and deformable limits their translation into wearable applications. Future designs are expected to shift support to long-term static monitoring, such as plant acoustics, in an energy-efficient, preamplifier-free manner[94].

Beyond the fundamental transduction mechanisms discussed above, bioacoustic sensors also differ in their integration platforms and operating modalities. Microelectromechanical systems (MEMS) technology represents a miniaturized fabrication and integration platform that can incorporate piezoelectric, capacitive, piezoresistive, or electromagnetic transduction mechanisms. Ultrasonic sensing, in contrast, refers to an acoustic frequency regime and application modality, typically relying on piezoelectric or capacitive transducers for high-frequency wave emission and reception. Therefore, MEMS integration and ultrasonic sensing are discussed here as cross-cutting architectures rather than parallel sensing mechanisms. 3.3.1 Toward MEMS integration and hybridization MEMS has revolutionized acoustic sensing through miniaturization, mass production, and integration of multiple transduction mechanisms within a unified platform. By leveraging mature silicon processing and thin-film deposition, MEMS microphones achieve excellent reproducibility and low power consumption. However, their conventional rigid architecture and high resonant frequency (typically >1 kHz) are poorly matched to the low-frequency regime of human body acoustics. To address this, recent works have introduced flexible MEMS architectures that integrate soft materials (PI, PDMS, TPU) with functional films (PZT, PVDF, graphene). For example, an origami-inspired flexible electromagnetic MEMS sensor surrounded by a flexible coil and a circular vibrator can achieve a broadband (1–10 kHz) response and conformal adhesion to the skin[95]. Although its output voltage (~12 μV) remains low, the design demonstrates the feasibility of integrating magnetomechanical conversion in wearable form. Similarly, multilayer graphene diaphragms incorporated into MEMS microphones have achieved sensitivities up to 24 mV·Pa⁻¹ with reduced stiffness and improved compliance[96]. Piezoelectric MEMS sensors represent another major advance, combining selfpowered operation with microfabrication precision. Flexible single-crystal PZT films and rib-structured diaphragms significantly enhance piezoelectric coupling and mechanical stability, achieving sensitivities of 36 mV·Pa⁻¹ and SNRs exceeding 50 dB[96]. Such devices are particularly promising for miniaturized stethoscopes, wearable patches, and implantable health monitors. Piezoresistive MEMS variants using graphene or porous semiconductors further extend capabilities for detecting subtle laryngeal or vocal cord vibrations[97].

Despite these achievements, critical challenges persist. Rigid MEMS structures are inherently limited in accommodating the skin’s curvature, leading to signal distortion and poor acoustic coupling. Moreover, the sensitivity and bandwidth trade-off remains a major bottleneck: thin diaphragms offer a wide frequency response but reduce the displacement amplitude, while thick films improve the sensitivity but narrow the bandwidth. Future research must therefore adopt hybrid transduction strategies such as integrating piezoelectric and piezoresistive effects within a single MEMS diaphragm to exploit complementary advantages in sensitivity and dynamic range. Another emerging direction is soft–hard hybrid integration, where MEMS chips are embedded in elastomeric substrates to achieve localized rigidity for sensing while maintaining global flexibility (Figure 3(g)). This strategy not only improves user comfort but also facilitates array-level integration for spatially resolved bioacoustic imaging[77]. Additionally, the combination of MEMS with edge algorithms and wireless communication modules is redefining wearable diagnostics toward intelligent, self-adaptive sensing systems capable of real-time decision-making under complex physiological conditions.
3.3.2 Ultrasonic sensing transducers and high-frequency acoustic modalities

Ultrasonic sensors are devices that exploit the propagation characteristics of ultrasonic waves in a medium to achieve sensing functionality, with their operational principle primarily rooted in the processes of emission, propagation, and reception of ultrasonic waves. In most biomedical and wearable ultrasound systems, piezoelectric transducers remain dominant because of their high electromechanical coupling

efficiency and fast response. Thus, piezoelectric ultrasonic sensors are better understood as piezoelectric transducers operating in the ultrasonic frequency range and optimized for both wave emission and echo reception[98]. Most piezoelectric ultrasonic transducers adopt a sandwich structure composed of a piezoelectric active layer, top and bottom electrodes, acoustic matching layers, and backing layers[99]: PZT or piezoelectric composites are commonly used as active elements. Matching layers reduce acoustic impedance mismatches and improve coupling with the target medium, while backing layers absorb backward waves and enhance axial resolution. Therefore, the material composition and thickness of these layers are key parameters for balancing sensitivity, bandwidth, and imaging resolution[100].

With the continuous advancement of intelligent sensing technologies, rigid ultrasonic transducers, distinguished by their high precision and stability, have assumed a pivotal role in the field of biomedical engineering. Yin et al. proposed a typical rigid ultrasonic transducer based on 1-3 piezoelectric composites, which is used for prosthetic control[101]. This is a common sandwich structure with a customized thickness of the matching layer, backing layer and shell, which has already been used in their previous research[102-104]. To address the limitations of rigid transducers, Sgambato et al. explored a flexible modular A-mode ultrasound armband with dry silicone coupling, enabling wrist-hand tracking and demonstrating the great potential and generalization capacity of ultrasound-based technology as a virtual reality interface (Figure 4(a)[105].

Despite the technical foundation laid by these works, the inherent limitations of rigid transducers remain prominent, including fixed geometric dimensions, inflexible structural forms, and poor conformal contact with human skin, which severely restrict their long-term wearable applicability in unconstrained daily scenarios. When transitioned to flexible or soft architectures, ultrasonic transducers retain muscle status monitoring capabilities while achieving better conformal contact with human skin; compared to rigid counterparts, flexible substrates exhibit enhanced wear resistance and long-term comfort. For instance, Gao et al. developed a fully integrated wearable ultrasonic myography system with a thickness reduced to approximately 2 mm, significantly improving comfort and usability (Figure 4(b))[106]. Another type of ultrasound transducer was proposed by Toymus et al. for bladder volume monitoring. It has a design of air-backing, which eliminates energy loss due to absorptive backing layers and allows ultrasonic sensing with lower voltages, realizing high accuracy detection in volunteers with various bladder shapes and sizes (Figure 4(c))[107]. Similarly, Zhang et al. proposed another kind of conformable ultrasound sensor based on multiple phased arrays for bladder volume monitoring (Figure 4(d))[1]. In this work, two matching layers are designed for better matching with human skin, and a thick nonconductive backing layer outside the electrodes is set for sound wave oscillation absorption, which is different from the structure developed by Gao et al.[106], whose conductive backing layer is between the piezoelectric component and electrodes.

Moreover, for blood flow or blood pressure monitoring, ultrasonic sensors can also play an important role. As an example, a transducer array was designed by Wang et al., which is still a sandwich structure with a flexible substrate and electrode (Figure 4(e))[108]. To improve the breathability and wearability, Noda et al. proposed a kind of textile-based ultrasound imaging probe (Figure 4(f)). Compared to previous probes, this probe can show good performance in B-mode imaging because of the size and arrangement of piezoelectric components. On the other hand, it shows great potential to integrate ultrasound sensors into common cloth for daily monitoring [109].

3.4 Critical analysis and trade-offs in sensor selection

Different transduction categories with various mechanisms exhibit distinct advantages for specific bioacoustic targets. Piezoelectric and triboelectric sensors, characterized by high sensitivity, fast response, and mechanical compliance, are most effective for human physiological monitoring, such as heart, lung, bowel, and laryngeal sound detection, where low-frequency (<2 kHz) vibrations dominate. Piezoresistive and capacitive sensors provide high resolution for microdeformation and are ideal for vocal or throat vibration monitoring and wearable e-skin systems requiring continuous contact and stretchability. MEMS microphones, with miniaturized and low-power operation, extend applications to both human and animal studies, supporting portable auscultation and wildlife sound recording.

Furthermore, bioacoustic sensors cannot be implemented as a one-size-fits-all universal solution. Their selection is inherently governed by a tripartite trade-off among mechanical compliance, electromechanical coupling efficiency, and frequency bandwidth. For instance, in human physiological monitoring, piezoelectric polymers such as PVDF or triboelectric nanogenerators are commonly adopted[60,69], rather than rigid ceramic materials such as lead zirconate titanate (PZT). Such design trade-offs deliberately sacrifice the ultrahigh energy conversion efficiency of rigid materials to achieve superior mechanical conformability, which is critical for minimizing acoustic impedance mismatch at the skin-sensor interface. In contrast, acoustic signals in plant research are extremely weak and fall within the high-frequency range of 20−150 kHz, thereby requiring

priority to be placed on detection sensitivity and bandwidth. Accordingly, rigid ultrasonic transducers or noncontact optical and electromagnetic sensors are widely utilized, despite their inherent lack of flexibility and stringent requirements for installation and alignment. Additionally, microelectromechanical system (MEMS) technology exhibits unparalleled miniaturization advantages for large-scale array deployment. Nevertheless, a critical design compromise remains: a thinner MEMS diaphragm is essential to broaden the frequency response range, which inevitably reduces vibration displacement and degrades the detection sensitivity toward typical ultralow-frequency vibrations (<100 Hz), such as heart sounds and bowel sounds. Consequently, MEMS sensors are rationally applicable only when the spatial resolution performance of sensor arrays outweighs the demand for ultralow-frequency peak sensitivity.

Collectively, the choice of transduction mechanism should align with the biological target, dominant frequency range, and required mechanical compliance, ensuring reliable signal acquisition across diverse bioacoustic systems. For reference, Table 1 summarizes representative sensor types, their primary targets, detection frequency ranges, key performance metrics, and potential applications. While advanced acoustic sensors provide the essential hardware foundation for capturing high-fidelity bioacoustic vibrations, the raw hardware output is frequently contaminated by environmental noise, motion artifacts, and overlapping crossspecies signals. Therefore, the leap from capturing raw physical vibrations to extracting meaningful biological insights cannot rely on hardware alone; it necessitates robust signal acquisition strategies and sophisticated downstream processing algorithms. To address this, Section 4 systematically explores the methodologies for bioacoustic signal acquisition and the artificial intelligence-driven analytical frameworks used to decode these complex acoustic signatures. 3.5 Technical bottlenecks in sensing performance

While the aforementioned transduction mechanisms provide the physical basis for bioacoustic sensing, translating these principles into high-performance wearable and field-deployable devices faces several fundamental technical bottlenecks. These challenges are primarily manifested in the inherent trade-offs among three key performance metrics: SNR, sensitivity, and frequency bandwidth. (1) Signal quality bottlenecks: the primary bottleneck for SNR in bioacoustics is the presence of high-intensity ambient noise and internal electronic noise floors. For wearable biomedical sensors, 1/f noise (flicker noise) at low frequencies severely interferes with the capture of heart and bowel sounds (typically <100 Hz). Moreover, as sensors are miniaturized to improve comfort, the reduction in active sensing area inherently leads to a higher thermal noise floor (Brownian noise), which limits the ability to resolve ultraweak signals, such as those from fetal heartbeats or deep-tissue acoustics. Current research aims to address this by developing differential noise-canceling architectures and specialized low-noise front-end amplifiers, yet achieving a high SNR in unstructured, chaotic environments remains a persistent challenge. (2) Sensitivity vs. dynamic range trade-offs: high sensitivity is essential for detecting subtle bioacoustic events such as plant xylem cavitation or early-stage pathological murmurs. However, increasing sensitivity often comes at the expense of a dynamic range. For instance, sensors optimized for high-sensitivity detection of weak signals may suffer from saturation or nonlinear distortion when exposed to high-amplitude sounds (e.g., loud vocalizations or industrial agricultural noise). The challenge lies in engineering materials with high electromechanical coupling coefficients (e.g., optimized PZT or high-performance ferroelectric polymers) that can maintain linear sensitivity across several orders of magnitude in pressure amplitude. (3) Frequency bandwidth constraints: Bioacoustic signals span a vast frequency range, from infrasonic animal communications (<20 Hz) to ultrasonic plant emissions (>20 kHz). Designing a single sensor that provides a flat, high-fidelity frequency response across this entire spectrum is a major engineering hurdle. Highsensitivity sensors often rely on mechanical resonance to amplify signals, which inherently limits their effective bandwidth. Conversely, broadening the bandwidth through mechanical damping inevitably degrades

the sensitivity and SNR. Furthermore, for MEMS-based acoustic sensors, the trade-off between the diaphragm’s stiffness (required for high-frequency response) and its compliance (required for low-frequency sensitivity) represents a critical structural bottleneck that currently necessitates the use of multisensor arrays or heterogeneous integration strategies to achieve broad-spectrum coverage.

Bioacoustic signals, serving as acoustic carriers of dynamic interactions within living systems, facilitate cross-disciplinary breakthroughs spanning life sciences to engineering applications. This section focuses on the acquisition of acoustic signals from humans, animals, and plants, systematically discussing the characteristic differences across biological systems, the innovative principles underlying acquisition technologies, and their representative application scenarios. Emphasis is placed on human physiological signal acquisition, high-sensitivity MEMS and flexible electronics integration paradigms within wearable devices, and the technological innovations of heterogeneous microphone arrays and fiber-optic sensing in ecological monitoring of fauna and flora. In summary, this delineates the continuum of bioacoustic technology from physiological signal capture to ecological behavior decoding. While the operational environments differ from the controlled clinical settings for human auscultation to the chaotic underwater acoustic channels for marine tracking, the fundamental goal of signal acquisition remains the same: maximizing the SNR and capturing high-fidelity acoustic signals.
4.1.1 Acquisition systems for human physiological sounds

As a dynamic mapping of physiological states, the precise acquisition of human physiological signals represents a core challenge in bioacoustics. Unlike the isolated sensor transduction mechanisms detailed in Section 3, modern acquisition systems emphasize the synergy between sensing elements, front-end signal conditioning, and wireless architectures.

To capture inherently weak physiological signals with high fidelity, system-level integration of functional materials and front-end circuitry is paramount. For instance, wearable acoustic systems based on micromechanical arrays [77] (Figure 5(a)) or self-powered auditory components [69] (Figure 5(b)) increasingly rely on integrated transimpedance amplification and deep negative-feedback circuits. These front-end architectures are essential to optimize signal conversion, broaden bandwidth, and minimize raw distortion[113-

115]. Furthermore, ensuring a high-quality acoustic interface requires conformal system designs. Epidermal sensing systems [116] (Figure 5(c)) and ultrathin vibration-sensitive electronic skins [117, 118] (Figure 5(d)) achieve excellent acoustic impedance matching with the human body, facilitating multimodal acquisition (e.g., concurrent speech and neck motion) while physically suppressing environmental noise loss at the skin-sensor interface.

Beyond the analog front-end, the integration of digital modules has enabled autonomous, wireless diagnostic platforms. Soft, wearable stethoscopes now routinely integrate signal processing electronics to support real-time disease diagnosis directly on the edge [111] (Figure 5(e)). Similarly, Wang introduced a wireless acoustic patch featuring a microbattery, Bluetooth module, and a bidirectional microphone configuration [119] (Figure 5(f)). This architectural design employs system-level signal separation algorithms to isolate internal bowel acoustics from ambient interference, pushing the boundary of unobtrusive monitoring.

At a higher level of complexity, multidevice networks and active noise-suppression architectures are redefining physiological acquisition. Prof. Rogers’ group developed an epidermal acoustic interface system[48] enabled by a multidevice time-synchronization network (Figure 5(g)). It utilizes dual-microphone adaptive filtering to achieve real-time, synchronized spatiotemporal mapping of cardiopulmonary dynamics across multiple anatomical sites. Additionally, addressing motion artifacts at the system level is crucial; Prof. Chen’s

group designed a self-filtering acoustic system utilizing a permanent fluidic magnet network [112, 120] (Figure 5(h)). By leveraging acoustic-magnetic coupling, the system inherently suppresses low-frequency motion artifacts below 30 Hz, transforming acoustic acquisition into a robust platform capable of functioning in chaotic real-world environments.

Despite recent advancements, human physiological signal acquisition still faces challenges. Persistent issues such as environmental noise interference, interindividual physiological variability, limitations in device portability and user comfort, and concerns over data privacy continue to hinder widespread clinical and translational adoption. Specifically, divergent acquisition strategies across humans, animals, and plants are driven by the specific operational constraints of each domain. In human wearable acoustics, the primary design decision is to combat motion artifacts. Researchers often choose dual-microphone architectures (inwardfacing and outward-facing); the trade-off is that while this significantly improves the SNR through active noise cancellation, it doubles the data throughput and power consumption, challenging the battery life of miniaturized patches. In ecological monitoring, the paradigm shifts from single-node fidelity to spatial coverage. Heterogeneous microphone arrays are predominantly chosen to track wildlife. However, the critical trade-off in array design is spatial resolution versus data transmission bottleneck. A dense 64-micron array provides exceptional localization but generates massive, continuous audio files that cannot be transmitted over limited wireless networks in remote habitats, necessitating high-power local storage solutions. For plant ultrasonic acquisition, the necessity to sample at >300 kHz (to capture up to 150 kHz signals) strictly dictates the use of wired, lab-based high-speed data acquisition systems, explaining why autonomous, field-deployable plant acoustic sensors remain remarkably scarce.

Addressing these hurdles requires a holistic approach that integrates innovations in functional material design, system-level integration, and intelligent algorithmic frameworks. Future efforts should aim to enable real-time sensing with high sensitivity and low noise under complex physiological conditions while accommodating personalized needs. Such advances are expected to catalyze transformative progress in medical diagnostics and human–machine interaction.

4.1.2 Acquisition systems for animal sound signals

The acquisition of animal acoustic signals has evolved from opportunistic single-species recordings to structured, large-scale ecological surveillance systems. The core of these macroscopic acquisition systems lies in scalable, high-spatial-resolution architectures rather than individual sensor performance. Heterogeneous microphone arrays stand out as a cornerstone for high-spatial-resolution and noninvasive terrestrial monitoring. Verreychen developed a scalable, dense 64-microphone array to localize vocalizing animals in natural habitats (Figure 6(a))[121]. This system resolved fine details of echolocation beams in foraging pale bats and simultaneously tracked multiple songbird species within a 75-meter radius, offering a robust tool for longterm, large-scale biodiversity conservation. Complementarily, Mennill designed a portable wireless array— comprising four GPS-synchronized stereo recorders with omnidirectional microphones—for field-based multichannel data capture[122]. Deployed in open and forested environments, it achieved a sound source localization accuracy of (1.87 ± 0.13) m across 25 animal vocalizations, clarifying how microphone spacing, habitat type, and source position influence precision and providing a low-cost solution for spatial behavior studies.

Cross-species auditory research leverages specialized tools to unravel biomechanical mechanisms. Ding used a laser Doppler vibrometer (LDV) to quantify stapes vibration changes in live guinea pigs with endolymphatic hydrops (Figure 6(b))[123], revealing the biomechanical basis of Meniere’s disease-related hearing loss and establishing a reference for cross-species auditory studies. For insect monitoring, Turov employed distributed acoustic sensors (DAS) with fiber-optic arrays to capture signals from Madagascar hissing cockroaches, achieving centimeter-scale localization (Figure 6(c))[124] and opening new avenues for insect behavioral research. Frommolt further integrated long-term monitoring with automation: a 5-year wetland study used four quad-channel recorders with cardioid microphones to track Eurasian bittern nocturnal calls[125]. A 140 Hz sine wave template enabled automatic call detection, while time-difference-of-arrival (TDOA) algorithms and microphone directionality facilitated individual spatial tracking, forming an integrated framework for cryptic bird population monitoring.

Animals perceive a broader acoustic spectrum (infrasound <20 Hz to ultrasound >20 kHz) than humans, but capturing these signals has long been constrained by issues such as cost, power consumption, and portability. Okamoto proposed a compact, energy-efficient 4-channel microphone array (ChirpArray) designed specifically for long-term outdoor recording, which offers significant advantages in ecoacoustic monitoring (Figure 6(d))[126]. Its ultralow power consumption enables efficient and flexible deployment, making it an ideal solution for expanding field monitoring and large-scale landscape recording. Stoeger combined acoustic cameras with linear predictive coding (LPC) and machine learning (ML) to capture African elephant vocalizations during separation and reunion (Figure 6(e))[127]. Frame-by-frame analysis distinguished “trunk calls” from “oral calls,” with >97% classification accuracy, providing a multiscale paradigm for studying low-frequency acoustic biomechanics.

Marine bioacoustic detection is more complex due to water’s variable sound-propagation properties, driving the integration of sonar and flexible electronics. Kinck used a hydrophone-equipped autonomous underwater glider (Seaglider) for near-real-time monitoring of deep-sea species such as beaked whales (Figure 6(f))[128]. Month-long deployments integrated salinity/temperature data to map cetacean distributions,
although bandwidth limits and ocean reverberation remain unresolved.

Recent advances have expanded marine capabilities: Song combined CT scanning and ultrasonic measurements to reconstruct sound velocity in Indo-Pacific humpback dolphin forehead tissues (Figure 6(g), upper)[129], suggesting that dolphins optimize sound focusing via thermoregulation (37 °C body temperature), informing biomimetic temperature-compensated acoustic devices. Duarte reviewed anthropogenic impacts on marine soundscapes (Figure 6(g), lower[3], highlighting vessel/industrial noise disruption of cetacean/fish communication and positioning acoustic monitoring as key for ecological health tracking. Barroso applied ML to classify fish vocalizations[130], enabling large-scale marine surveys. Tian developed a self-powered, alloptical underwater ultrasonic sensor (SAWS) via triboelectric-induced electroluminescence[131], pioneering microscale acoustic visualization. For deep-sea benthic monitoring, Masmitja deployed a mobile robotic platform with acoustic receivers (Figure 6(h))[132], using long-baseline (LBL) positioning and TDOA algorithms to track tagged Norway lobsters (400 m depth, 3 months). Clock drift calibration via static receivers/dynamic robots achieved meter-scale precision, offering a scalable solution for deep-sea acoustic acquisition.

When evaluating these ecological sensing strategies, distinct trade-offs emerge between static passive acoustic monitoring (PAM) and mobile autonomous platforms. While PAM nodes (e.g., ChirpArray) offer low-power, long-term temporal continuity, they are limited by a fixed “listening radius” and struggle with spatial blind spots in complex terrains[126]. In contrast, mobile platforms such as Seagliders provide spatial flexibility but introduce significant self-noise from propulsion systems and flow, necessitating advanced blindsource separation algorithms. Furthermore, the validation of these systems remains a major bottleneck. Unlike clinical diagnostics that use ECG as a gold standard, ecological validation relies on expert manual annotation of spectrograms or visual confirmation via camera traps, both of which are labor intensive and prone to observer bias. Future systems must move toward “multimodal ground-truth” fusion, integrating acoustic data with environmental DNA (eDNA) or GPS-tagged biomechanical sensors to cross-validate species presence and behavioral interpretation.

In conclusion, animal acoustic acquisition technologies now span terrestrial and marine domains: heterogeneous arrays enable precise terrestrial localization, LDV/DAS unravel auditory mechanisms/microbehaviors, and low-cost infrasound/acoustic cameras overcome frequency detection barriers. Marine innovations (gliders, robots, all-optical sensors) extend deep-sea monitoring. Future progress requires addressing environmental interference and cross-scale coordination; low-cost, intelligent solutions will drive integrated “terrestrial-marine” networks, supporting global ecological conservation.

4.1.3 Plant acoustics and health monitoring systems

Plant acoustics, a pivotal frontier in bioacoustics, is unraveling hidden acoustic communication networks. Technologically, modern plant bioacoustic acquisition is increasingly characterized by the development of AIoT (artificial intelligence of things) platforms, which require high-speed data acquisition architectures capable of capturing ultrasonic emissions (>20 kHz). Understanding plant acoustic behavior begins with perception mechanisms. Demey elucidated that plants sense environmental acoustic signals (e.g., insect wingbeat frequencies) via mechanically sensitive membrane ion channels (Figure 7(a))[133]. This perception modulates physiological processes (e.g., stomatal movement) and plant-insect ecological networks, laying a molecular foundation for functional studies of plant acoustic signals. Toyota revealed that glutamate-triggered, calcium-dependent long-distance defense pathways are enhanced by stimulus-induced ion channels, amplifying defense gene expression (Figure 7(b))[134]]. This advances defense research from signal description to mechanistic analysis, hinting at uncharacterized links between acoustic vibrations and plant defense. Mishra further synthesized plant acoustic responses, showing that acoustic vibrations alter membrane protein structures, microfilament arrangement, and calcium signaling, initiating molecular cascades that regulate gene expression and growth[135]. Their proposed signal transduction model (Figure 7(c)) provides a theoretical framework for acoustic signal acquisition and plant health monitoring.

Stress-induced plant acoustics is a core focus. Khait used a microphone array to capture 20–150 kHz ultrasonic signals from drought-stressed tomato plants, with spectral traits correlating with water deficit (Figure 7(d))[[136], establishing a noncontact monitoring paradigm. Waqas, Khait, and colleagues further found that plants emit species-, stress type-, and severity-specific ultrasonic signals under drought, wounding, or viral infection (Figure 7(e))[40]; these signals, potentially perceivable by animals, hold promise for precision agriculture[137]. Technologically, Bonisoli developed a low-cost ultrasonic microphone system (20–100 kHz, covering key plant emission bands)[138], leveraging open-source software and a single microphone to boost practical applicability. Nardini reviewed over a century of plant acoustics research, noting that sounds primarily originate from physical processes such as xylem cavitation (Figure 7(f))[139], but direct evidence for plant-animal/plant‒plant acoustic communication remains speculative. Research has extended to marine ecosystems: Ostrovsky used high-frequency echosounding to monitor cyanobacterial blooms, analyzing echo differences between intact and collapsed Microcystis gas vesicles (Figure 7(g))[140]. Gas vesicles enhance acoustic scattering, enabling real-time spatiotemporal tracking of Microcystis—supporting cyanobacterial bloom prediction and aquatic ecosystem protection.

Current plant acoustics have a framework spanning molecular perception to ecological applications but face hurdles: signal complexity (environmental noise, multisource coupling) and unclear cross-species communication mechanisms. Future work should integrate genomics, acoustic engineering, and AI, build stress-specific standardized acoustic databases, and translate laboratory findings to precision agriculture/ecological conservation, deepening plant biology understanding and offering transformative solutions for global agricultural and ecological challenges.
