7.4 Comparative analysis of cross-domain technical challenges

While the abovementioned sections highlight the transformative applications of bioacoustics across clinical diagnostics, human‒machine interfaces (HMI), and precision agriculture, a horizontal comparison reveals several shared, fundamental technical bottlenecks that currently limit broad commercial translation. Rather than isolated issues, these challenges manifest distinctively across different operational domains: (1) Motion artifact suppression and environmental noise robustness: in real-world deployments, target bioacoustic signals are invariably corrupted by noise. For clinical stethoscopes (Section 7.1) and HMI devices (Section 7.2), the primary interference stems from low-frequency motion artifacts (e.g., body movements, skin friction) and ambient conversation. Current solutions rely heavily on acoustic impedance matching materials or differential microphone arrays to isolate signals. Conversely, in agriculture and ecology (Section 7.3), the noise profile is highly unstructured and dominated by wind, rain, and agricultural machinery. Suppressing these broad-spectrum interferences requires transitioning from physical shielding to adaptive, AI-driven noise cancellation algorithms capable of functioning in chaotic open-field conditions. (2) Trade-offs between power consumption and system integration: the shift from wired data acquisition to wireless, continuous monitoring creates a severe power-integration dilemma. Wearable medical patches and HMI voice-recognition interfaces demand ultrasmall form factors, strictly limiting battery capacity. This necessitates the development of ultralow-power microcontrollers or self-powered triboelectric/piezoelectric acoustic sensors. For agricultural AIoT networks, while size constraints are relatively relaxed, the sensors must operate autonomously for months in remote fields. Therefore, integrating computationally intensive edge-AI modules for real-time acoustic classification (to avoid transmitting massive raw audio files via LoRa) without depleting the energy budget remains a critical architectural trade-off. (3) Cross-subject and cross-environment generalization: a ubiquitous challenge across all bioacoustic applications is the degradation of machine learning model performance when transitioning from training datasets to unseen subjects or environments. In clinical and HMI applications, algorithms trained on specific cohorts often fail when applied to individuals with varying body mass indices (BMIs), anatomical variations, or distinct vocal timbres. Similarly, in agricultural applications, ultrasonic stress emission models trained on specific plant species in controlled chambers struggle to generalize to diverse crops in open fields with varying soil and atmospheric conditions. Overcoming this generalization gap urgently requires large-scale, standardized, and multicenter acoustic databases coupled with advanced domain adaptation and transfer learning techniques.

By recognizing these shared technical hurdles, future research can foster cross-disciplinary solutions— such as transferring robust motion-suppression algorithms from wearable health devices to agricultural monitoring nodes—thereby accelerating the maturity of bioacoustic sensing networks.

Despite significant developments in acoustic sensing and signal processing, the advancement of bioacoustics faces multifaceted challenges. This section outlines a roadmap for future bioacoustic research by examining key bottlenecks in hardware, signal processing, data resources, and system integration, followed by targeted research directions to address these limitations.

(1) Hardware and sensing limitations: the primary physical bottleneck across domains is acoustic impedance mismatch and signal attenuation. In medical monitoring, soft tissues act as severe low-pass filters, dampening high-frequency pathological features, while wearable sensors suffer from motion artifacts and sweat-induced degradation. In ecological and agricultural applications, sensors face extreme environmental degradation (e.g., biofouling in oceans, extreme temperatures) and struggle to capture ultraweak signals (e.g., 20-150 kHz plant emissions) without invasive deployment. (2) Signal processing and algorithmic constraints: current algorithms lack robustness against nonstationary interference. In human‒machine interfaces (HMIs), extracting weak vocal signals amidst ambient conversational noise remains difficult without distorting the target signal. Similarly, in wildlife monitoring, separating specific species from a “cocktail party” of overlapping multispecies vocalizations, wind, and anthropogenic noise requires massive computational power that far exceeds the capacity of remote nodes.

(3) Data scarcity and lack of standardization: severe “labeling crisis” plagues bioacoustics. Unlike general audio, annotating clinical murmurs or rare avian calls requires specialized expertise, leading to small, biased datasets. Furthermore, cross-domain applications suffer from a lack of standardized, open-access databases and rigorous testing frameworks. This is particularly evident in plant acoustics, where the mechanistic correlation between acoustic emissions and biological functions remains controversial due to inconsistent data collection.

(4) System integration and deployment: the transition from wired laboratory setups to wireless, continuous monitoring creates a severe power-integration dilemma. Wearable patches demand ultrasmall form factors with strictly limited battery capacity, while agricultural AIoT nodes must operate autonomously for months. Transmitting massive raw acoustic data over limited bandwidths (e.g., LoRa or underwater acoustic channels) further paralyzes real-time system integration.
To unlock the full potential of bioacoustics and address the aforementioned bottlenecks, future research should be strategically directed across the following corresponding dimensions:

(1) Hardware innovation (Edge-AI and self-powered sensors): future developments should focus on embedding ultralow-power microcontrollers directly onto conformable acoustic patches for real-time, onsensor anomaly detection (e.g., arrhythmia alerts). For ecological applications, integrating energy-harvesting technologies (e.g., triboelectric, solar, or bioenergy) into mobile robotic platforms (drones, gliders) is critical to achieving battery-free, long-term deployment.

(2) Signal processing (Multimodal Fusion and Explainable AI): to overcome motion artifacts and noise, algorithms must evolve toward multimodal architectures that inherently fuse acoustic data with electrophysiological (ECG/EMG), kinematic (IMU), or environmental signals. Additionally, developing explainable AI (XAI) is urgent to translate “black-box” acoustic feature representations into physiologically grounded, clinical, or ecological insights.

(3) Data strategies (self-supervised learning and federated databases): to solve the data annotation bottleneck, research must leverage self-supervised learning (SSL) paradigms that pretrain foundation models on massive unlabeled physiological and ecological audio. Simultaneously, global efforts must prioritize establishing standardized, multicenter, open-access databases that correlate acoustic spectral signatures with rigorous ground truths (e.g., multiomics data in plants or clinical imaging in humans).

(4) System-level integration (AIoT and closed-loop frameworks): the ultimate trajectory is the deployment of intelligent, networked systems. In precision agriculture, this means deploying low-cost ultrasonic microphone arrays alongside soil and weather sensors within an AIoT framework to create automated, closed-loop irrigation and pest control systems. In ecology, integrating federated learning across decentralized mobile networks will enable global-scale biodiversity mapping without the transmission bottleneck of raw audio.

Acoustic sensing technologies, encompassing both bioacoustics and biomedical acoustics, have evolved from a niche research field to a transformative technology with far-reaching implications for healthcare, ecology, and beyond. This review has charted the rapid advancements in bioacoustic sensing (from piezoelectric transducers to MEMS devices) and signal processing (from traditional feature engineering to deep learning), highlighting their roles in decoding human physiology, animal behavior, and plant ecology. The interdisciplinary nature of bioacoustics—bridging acoustics, biology, materials science, and artificial intelligence—has enabled breakthroughs in noninvasive monitoring, from intelligent stethoscopes for cardiac disease diagnosis to acoustic camera systems for biodiversity tracking.

Despite significant progress, challenges in noise resilience, sensor miniaturization, vocal mechanisms and data standardization must be addressed to realize the full potential of bioacoustics. The integration of AI, flexible electronics, and multimodal sensing frameworks offers a roadmap for future innovations. The true potential of next-generation bioacoustics lies not in isolated advancements within medical or ecological silos but in the translation of technologies across these boundaries. The cross-pollination of sensor designs and AI models among human, animal, and plant acoustics will be the catalyst for the next paradigm shift. Looking ahead, bioacoustics is poised to play a central role in solving global challenges, from early disease detection in resource-constrained settings to monitoring climate change impacts on ecosystems. By fostering crossdisciplinary collaboration and prioritizing technological standardization, the field can unlock new frontiers in understanding life systems and driving sustainable development. The next decade promises to witness bioacoustics emerge as a cornerstone of precision medicine, smart agriculture, and ecological conservation, shaping a more interconnected and responsive world.

figures.label: Figure 1
figures.caption_original: Figure 1. Overview of the origin, classification, and propagation of bioacoustic signals in biological species. (a) Origin and classification of sound. (b) Sound propagation in biological species. Depicts sound propagation characteristics and acoustic signal acquisition strategies across humans, animals, and plants. For humans, it includes vocal sounds from the throat (ranging from 20 to 2 kHz) and internal acoustic signals generated by organs such as the cardiopulmonary system, stomach, and bowel. For animals, it covers broadband acoustic signals utilized in sensing and communication. For plants (exemplified by tomatoes, etc.), it illustrates acoustic signal propagation within internal structures (e.g., xylem, cambium, phloem) and corresponding detection methods. Additionally, cross-sectional/profiled views (e.g., of the human thorax and plant tissues) visualize how acoustic signals propagate, reflect, and transmit in biological tissues.
